US House of Representatives may vote to impeach Defence Secy Hegseth. How it will work

A resolution has been introduced by Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie with eight articles of impeachment, including carrying out hostilities against Iran without a declaration of war.

Gregory Korte

10 November, 2026 12:59 pm IST

The House of Representatives could soon hold a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Though presidential impeachments get bigger headlines — Senate trials of Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton and Donald Trump (twice) transfixed the country — the House has also impeached cabinet secretaries and federal judges. The process can differ, but the underlying constitutional requirements are the same.

Who may be impeached, and for what?

Show Full Article

The Constitution holds that “The President, Vice President and all civil Officers of the United States, shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.”

What is an impeachable offense?

Treason and bribery are easily defined terms under federal law, but there’s long been a debate about the meaning of “high crimes and misdemeanors.” As Congress has defined it through the years, the phrase “high crimes and misdemeanors” includes exceeding or abusing the powers of office and misusing the office for improper purpose or gain.

Offenses don’t have to be criminal. Arguing for the adoption of the Constitution in Federalist No. 65, Alexander Hamilton defined impeachable offenses as “those offenses which proceed from the misconduct of public men, or, in other words, from the abuse or violation of some public trust.”

What are the allegations against Hegseth?

Representative Thomas Massie, the Kentucky Republican who lost a primary election this year to a Trump-backed challenger, introduced on Nov. 9 a resolution with eight articles of impeachment:

Hegseth carried out hostilities against Iran without a declaration of war and without an attack on the US.

He kept US forces fighting in Iran after both chambers passed a resolution directing their removal under the War Powers Resolution of 1973.

He continued the Iran war after the 60-day deadline for the president to withdraw forces unless authorized by Congress.

He dismantled legal civilian-protection safeguards, leading to a missile strike on an Iranian elementary school that killed at least 156 people, mostly children.

He directed unauthorized strikes against suspected drug boats in the Caribbean Sea and the Eastern Pacific that killed at least 243 people, denying quarter and rescue to survivors.

He retaliated against Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat, for his “you can refuse illegal orders” video directed at US military and intelligence personnel by threatening a court-martial, suppressing Kelly’s free speech rights.

He directed the raid that captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, an act of war not authorized by Congress.

He waged military operations in Yemen that killed an estimated 224 civilians, without congressional authorization or an imminent threat to the US.

Massie’s resolution is the third to target Hegseth. Two previous Democratic resolutions have failed to get a hearing in committee.

Thomas Massie | Bloomberg How has Hegseth responded?

In a social media post on Nov. 5, Hegseth defended his record in implementing Trump’s agenda.

“This is not about me, but of course the other side, in case you’ve noticed — they’re obsessed,” he said. “A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly.”

He portrayed the impeachment effort as part of a larger culture war, but also defended Trump’s military actions.

“Narco terrorists should die, not be caught and released,” he said, referring to the US’s series of lethal strikes against vessels that the military says are involved in drug trafficking. “When we say that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, we actually mean it, and we will do the hard work to ensure it.”

How does such an impeachment work?

The introduction of articles of impeachment is just the beginning of the process. Under House rules, an impeachment resolution is referred to the Judiciary Committee, currently led by close Trump ally Jim Jordan of Ohio.

But such resolutions can also be privileged, meaning that Massie or any other member may ask for a direct vote on the measure, bypassing committee. Such a vote must then take place within two legislative days. The House could also elect to “table” it rather than vote on the impeachment resolution itself, which would kill it before it goes to a vote.

If passed by a majority of the House, the impeachment then goes to the Senate for a trial, during which House “managers” serve as prosecutors. Senate trials of cabinet members work similarly to presidential impeachments except for one key difference: The chief justice of the US Supreme Court presides when the president is the defendant, since a vice president would have a conflict in a trial that could elevate him. Otherwise the Senate’s own presiding officer runs the proceedings. That could be Vice President JD Vance or, in his absence, president pro tempore Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican.

The full Senate need not stop its business to hold a trial. Under a 1935 rule, smaller panels of about 12 senators can hear evidence and then report findings to the full Senate.

Conviction and removal from office requires a two-thirds vote of all senators present. The Senate is controlled by Republicans until the next Congress convenes on Jan. 3, and even once Democrats take over the chamber, their majority will not be large enough to convict without some Republicans joining.

What happens if Congress adjourns before a trial?

If the House adjourns without a vote on the articles of impeachment, they’d have to be reintroduced in the next Congress. Under Democratic control, the House would likely be even more receptive to impeachment next year, but the involvement of a Republican sponsor such as Massie cloaks the effort as bipartisan.

The Senate moves slower, and a Senate trial would be as long or short as the chamber decides. Unlike the House, the Senate is a continuing body. There’s precedent for an impeachment by the House in one Congress to be decided by the Senate in the next: Most recently Judge Alcee Hastings, impeached in 1988 on bribery charges and convicted in 1989.

At the impeachment trial of President Andrew Johnson in 1868, the Senate acquitted him of three articles but then adjourned before deciding the other eight.

How common are impeachments of cabinet members?

Only two cabinet members have been impeached by the House: Secretary of War William Belknap for accepting kickbacks in 1876, and Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas over border enforcement in 2024. Belknap resigned and was acquitted by the Senate; the Senate dismissed the case against Mayorkas without a trial, sustaining a point of order that the accusations did not “allege conduct that rises to the level of a high crime or misdemeanor.”

Fourteen judges and one Supreme Court justice have been impeached throughout history. Eight of them have been found guilty — the most recent being G. Thomas Porteous Jr., a federal judge from Louisiana removed from office in 2010 for perjury and for accepting bribes.

Why Pete Hegseth faces impeachment and the 8 charges against him

A Republican-led impeachment push has put Donald Trump’s defence secretary under scrutiny over US military operations abroad.

Raunaq Lekhi

10 November, 2026 11:56 am IST

Follow Us:

-->

U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks during a briefing on the Iran war | Reuters/Kevin Lamarque

New Delhi: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing an impeachment push led by Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, who has accused him of violating the Constitution through his handling of American military operations in Iran, Yemen and Venezuela.

The resolution, introduced on 9 November, contains eight articles of impeachment . Three concern the war with Iran, while the remaining five deal with civilian casualties, military strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats, alleged retaliation against a US senator and military action in Venezuela and Yemen.

The move is significant because it comes from within President Donald Trump’s Republican Party, rather than solely from Democratic lawmakers. Massie has argued that Hegseth knowingly carried out unlawful military orders and poses a threat to the Constitution.

Show Full Article

However, these are allegations contained in an impeachment resolution, not findings of guilt. Hegseth has rejected the accusations and defended the administration’s military operations.

The eight articles explained 1. Waging war against Iran without congressional approval

The first article accuses Hegseth of helping launch the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran on 28 February 2026 without a declaration of war or specific authorisation from Congress. It invokes the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which limits the circumstances in which a President can commit American forces to hostilities without congressional approval.

2. Ignoring Congress’s order to withdraw troops

The second article alleges that Hegseth continued military operations in Iran despite Congress passing a concurrent resolution directing the withdrawal of US forces. The House approved the measure on 3 June and the Senate on 23 June. The article further accuses Hegseth of continuing hostilities from 26 June onwards, disregarding Congress’s direction.

3. Continuing the Iran war beyond the 60-day limit

The third article focuses on the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day deadline. Under the law, the President must terminate the use of American forces within 60 days of notifying Congress about their deployment, unless lawmakers authorise the operation or extend the deadline. The impeachment resolution says the deadline expired on 1 May, with a possible additional 30-day withdrawal period also expiring on 1 June. It alleges that Hegseth continued the campaign beyond both deadlines.

4. Weakening safeguards against civilian casualties

The fourth article accuses Hegseth of dismantling safeguards meant to protect civilians during military operations. It cites cuts to civilian casualty monitoring, changes to military legal oversight and the rollback of policies designed to reduce civilian harm.

It also points to the bombing of a girls’ school in Minab, Iran, on 28 February, which killed at least 156 people, including schoolchildren and teachers, according to the resolution. It argues that the alleged dismantling of safeguards contributed to the failure to prevent such casualties.

5. Killing suspected drug smugglers without trial

The fifth article concerns US military strikes on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. It alleges that Hegseth authorised attacks that killed at least 221 people, instead of allowing suspected smugglers to be intercepted, arrested and prosecuted.

It also highlights an incident in which a second strike allegedly killed survivors clinging to the wreckage of a boat after an initial attack. The resolution argues that these operations amounted to extrajudicial killings and violated laws governing military involvement in civilian law enforcement.

6. Retaliating against Senator Mark Kelly over free speech

The sixth article accuses Hegseth of using the Pentagon to intimidate Democratic Senator Mark Kelly, a retired Navy captain and former astronaut.

Kelly had appeared in a video in November 2025 telling American service members they could refuse illegal orders. The Pentagon subsequently threatened to recall him to active duty for possible court-martial proceedings and issued a letter of censure. The resolution argues that Hegseth’s actions violated Kelly’s First Amendment rights and amounted to retaliation against a sitting senator.

7. Seizing Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro

The seventh article concerns the US military operation that captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. It accuses Hegseth of overseeing an operation that amounted to an act of war against a sovereign country without congressional authorisation.

The resolution also alleges that the operation killed at least 83 people, including civilians, and went beyond the stated objective of apprehending a suspected criminal, effectively enabling regime change in Venezuela.

8. Launching an unauthorised military campaign in Yemen

The final article concerns Operation Rough Rider, the US military campaign against Yemen’s Houthi rebels between 15 March and 6 May 2025.

It alleges that Hegseth launched more than 1,100 strikes without the required congressional authorisation and that the campaign killed an estimated 224 civilians.

A key part of the charge concerns the Signal group chat controversy , in which Hegseth shared details of planned military strikes. The resolution cites messages in which Hegseth reportedly said the operation could easily be paused, arguing that this undermined the administration’s claim of an imminent threat requiring immediate military action.

What happens next? Impeachment does not automatically remove Hegseth from office. The House of Representatives must first approve the articles by a simple majority. If that happens, the case moves to the Senate, which holds a trial. Conviction and removal require a two-thirds majority of senators present.

Massie’s move has put Republican lawmakers in an uncomfortable position. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has backed the impeachment effort, while Trump has criticised Massie and defended Hegseth. House Speaker Mike Johnson has also opposed holding an impeachment vote while American forces remain engaged in hostilities abroad.

Hegseth, meanwhile, has dismissed the effort as politically motivated and said he is prepared to defend the administration’s military actions.

China’s trade surplus tops $1 trillion for second time ever as AI boom powers exports

This could fuel further tensions with EU, where leaders have called for more trade curbs with China after a pact with Beijing to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc.

Bloomberg News

10 November, 2026 11:08 am IST

Follow Us:

-->

Facebook

X

LinkedIn

WhatsApp

Email

Copy Link

The latest data mean China is headed for another year of a goods trade surplus in excess of $1 trillion. | Photographer: Qilai Shen/Bloomberg

Stay updated with ThePrint:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

-->

China’s trade surplus ballooned to just over $1 trillion for the year despite the biggest surge in imports since 2021, with an increasingly lopsided relationship with the European Union accounting for nearly a third of the overall imbalance.

Imports spiked far more than forecast and advanced almost 42% last month from a year earlier, data released by China’s General Administration of Customs showed on Tuesday. Shipments abroad rose slightly more than 35%, leaving the surplus for October at $105.3 billion, the smallest since May.

Through the first 10 months, China’s surplus is nearly 9% bigger than during the same period of last year, when it reached a record $1.2 trillion. In October, China exported $33.4 billion more to the EU than it imported from the bloc, bringing the year-to-date difference to more than $310 billion.

Show Full Article

China’s trade surplus “underscores the resilience and competitiveness of its export sector despite a more challenging global trade environment,” said Hao Zhou, chief economist at Guotai Junan International Holdings Ltd.

The entrenched imbalance in the flow of goods around China will stay high on the agenda of its biggest trading partners, with European leaders planning measures to manage what they deem to be economic security risks and tighten loopholes to better protect the bloc’s single market.

Top Beijing officials like Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang have pushed back by saying China would be importing more products if there weren’t restrictions on some high-tech items, saying it offers a market for countries and businesses around the world.

“Robust export and import growth in October again underscores the importance of tech manufacturing to China’s economy. It also highlights a vulnerability for a recovery that lacks support from domestic demand. The tech sector depends heavily on sales of AI-related hardware in foreign markets and, to a large extent, also operates as a processing hub. A drop in external demand — for example, if US data-center investment slows — could hit exports, a key engine of growth.”

Exports have soared this year thanks to surging global demand for AI hardware that’s also traded across Asia. While China’s imports also climbed, they still lag behind sales abroad, with gains largely confined to a few narrow products like gold in a sign of little rebound in domestic demand.

Rising concerns over the sustainability of the AI buildout boom are starting to cloud the outlook of China’s double-digit gains in exports. Chips and computer parts alone accounted for 40% of the year-on-year increase in Chinese export value so far, reflecting their soaring prices as a result of a building frenzy around data centers.

China’s export strength goes beyond AI hardware, however. In volume terms, growth came from a broad range of high-tech products, ranging from the “New Three” sectors promoted by China’s leadership — solar panels, electric vehicles and batteries — to industrial robots, according to a Goldman Sachs Group Inc. analysis.

In contrast, much of AI-related trade likely consists of assembling imported inputs and then re-exporting them, which limited its impact on the trade balance, Goldman Sachs economists found.

A rebound in China’s crude oil purchase is behind the surprising growth in imports. China imported nearly 42 million tons of crude in October, the highest amount since March. As oil prices climbed, the value of those imports hit a four-year high. Similarly, purchases of refined petroleum also jumped.

There were expectations that China’s state-run refiners would only start to replenish their oil stockpiles by increasing imports.

For exports, gains in high-tech goods accelerated to 67% last month from a year ago, the fastest since early 2021. Sales of chips and computers both soared at a triple-digit pace.

Shipments to the EU, the US and the Southeast Asian nations in the Asean group remained strong, growing at over 20%, 30% and 40% on year, respectively. Exports to the Netherlands, the UK and Brazil picked up strongly, according to the preliminary data, with sales to South Korea growing at a record pace.

(Updates with additional data details throughout. An earlier version of this story corrected the month in second paragraph.)

Centre questions Karnataka’s Ethanol testing process. So what is the prescribed procedure

The Centre has found fault with Karnataka’s sampling and testing methods used to claim that petrol contained 26-31 percent ethanol. ThePrint explains how ethanol content is supposed to be tested.

Udit Bubna

10 November, 2026 09:30 am IST

Follow Us:

-->

Facebook

X

LinkedIn

WhatsApp

Email

Copy Link

Representational image | Reuters

Stay updated with ThePrint:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

-->

New Delhi: India’s E20 programme requires oil marketing companies to ensure that petrol supplied to consumers meets prescribed ethanol-blending and fuel-quality standards, with ethanol content maintained within the 19–21 percent range. But verifying whether the fuel meets these standards depends not just on the laboratory conducting the test, but also on how samples are collected, handled and analysed.

Oil marketing companies (OMCs) allege that Karnataka’s October exercise deviated from the prescribed procedure. They say samples were collected without their representatives present and that they have not received the retained samples, outlet-wise details or laboratory reports.

These procedures have come under scrutiny following Karnataka’s Congress government claiming that petrol sold at certain retail outlets in the state contained 26–31 percent ethanol, significantly above the prescribed E20 limit of 20 percent ethanol.

Show Full Article

The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (MoPNG) and the three public sector OMCs—Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOCL), Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL) and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL)—have questioned both the sampling process and the laboratory methods used in Karnataka’s October 2026 exercise.

The latest controversy comes amid wider concerns over E20 petrol. In July, the policy faced criticism over possible mileage losses, particularly in older vehicles. The Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM) also flagged fuel-quality concerns, including chloride contamination and moisture, in a communication to the petroleum ministry. It later withdrew the communication, saying some figures needed further authentication.

EXPOSED: The document the Government tried hard to erase.

On July 28, 2026, SIAM officially warned the Union Govt that Excessive chloride in E20 petrol is actively damaging your vehicles.

Instead of protecting your hard earned money & your vehicles the govt went after news… pic.twitter.com/UEvExxS2jT

— Tehseen Poonawalla Official 🇮🇳 (@tehseenp) August 11, 2026

While the July debate centred on mileage and vehicle compatibility, the Karnataka controversy concerns whether petrol contained more ethanol than permitted. The process requires petrol samples to be collected and analysed in accordance with prescribed procedures.

According to Centre, these procedures are laid down under the Motor Spirit and High-Speed Diesel (Regulation of Supply, Distribution and Prevention of Malpractices) Order, 2005, issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, and the Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) 2024.

Under these rules, six one-litre samples must be collected from a petrol outlet. Two are handed to the dealer against acknowledgement, two are retained by the oil company or inspecting department, and the remaining two are sent to a laboratory specified under the control order.

Sample labels must be jointly signed, and test results communicated to the dealer and oil company within the prescribed timeframe. This allows all parties to verify the findings and seek retesting if they disagree.

The OMCs have also questioned the use of certificates from a third-party laboratory instead of a laboratory specified under the control order. The OMCs say the absence of samples and documentation has prevented them and the dealers from independently verifying the results or seeking a retest.

What methods should laboratories use? Even if samples are collected correctly, laboratories must follow prescribed technical standards to establish their ethanol content.

The relevant specification is identified under IS 17021:2018, the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) standard for ethanol-blended motor gasoline. The amendment, issued in August 2025, prescribes three methods for measuring ethanol content in E20 petrol.

The first is Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), which uses infrared light to identify and measure the concentration of substances in a fuel sample.

The second is water extraction method. Since ethanol mixes readily with water while petrol does not, this method uses water to separate ethanol from petrol before measuring its content through the prescribed procedure.

The third is Gas Chromatography, a laboratory technique that separates the different chemical components of a fuel sample so their individual quantities can be measured. It must follow the prescribed ASTM D4815 or D6839 standards. ASTM International is an organisation that develops standardised testing methods for materials and products.

Gas Chromatography also has specific requirements. The sample must first be diluted in equal proportions with oxygenate-free petrol, meaning petrol without ethanol or other oxygen-containing blending components. The result must then be corrected using an E10 certified reference material—a sample with a known composition used to check the accuracy of laboratory measurements.

The Centre says Karnataka’s laboratory certificates only mention that ethanol was measured using Gas Chromatography. They do not specify which ASTM standard was followed, whether the required dilution was carried out or which reference material was used.

Without these details, the reported ethanol levels of 26–31 percent cannot be independently validated against IS 17021, the Centre argues.

Why the Centre questioned the results The Ministry has questioned the density readings in Karnataka’s certificates. Since ethanol is denser than petrol, a higher ethanol proportion would ordinarily be expected to increase the fuel’s overall density.

Karnataka’s certificates recorded densities of 0.742–0.749 grams per cubic centimetre for samples reportedly containing 26-31 percent ethanol. In comparison, OMC tests of E20 samples recorded densities of 0.752–0.760 grams per cubic centimetre. The Centre says this difference warrants further examination through prescribed testing and comparison with appropriate reference samples.

The OMCs have also cited their nationwide quality-monitoring exercise conducted with the Centre for High Technology (CHT), under Petroleum Ministry. Of 893 samples collected from depots and retail outlets across 27 states and Union Territories, all were found to contain ethanol within the prescribed range of 19-21 percent.

This included 56 samples from Karnataka, covering all three OMCs and different locations. Their ethanol content ranged between 19 and 20 percent, averaging 19.30 percent.

The OMCs have sought Karnataka’s sampling records, laboratory reports and access to the samples. They have proposed joint testing at an authorised laboratory with representatives of both sides to establish whether the reported ethanol levels are accurate and meet the prescribed testing standards.

(Edited by Viny Mishra)
